title: ALK Inhibitor Response in Novel ZFPM2::ALK and TRIM24::ALK Fusion-Positive Lung Cancers: Case Report
author: Charles Hsu; Mohamed Yakoub; Michael Offin; Juliana Eng; Alexander Drilon; Soo-Ryum Yang
text:
Abstract
Background
ALK fusion-positive NSCLC is driven by a range of fusion partners, most often EML4::ALK. The clinical impact, oncogenicity, and resistance mechanisms of rare, noncanonical ALK fusions remain underexplored. We describe two previously unreported ALK fusion partners in NSCLC and explore the potential mechanisms of resistance in each case, including on-target and bypass mutations, as well as the use of next-generation sequencing (NGS) testing on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) as a useful tool.
Case Presentation
We report two patients with metastatic NSCLC harboring novel ZFPM2::ALK and TRIM24::ALK fusions. Both patients achieved marked partial responses to first-line alectinib, confirming the oncogenic and actionable nature of the fusions. The patient with ZFPM2::ALK fusion developed leptomeningeal disease after 27 months; CSF NGS revealed persistent fusion and newly acquired CDKN2A/B deletion. The patient with TRIM24::ALK fusion, following durable responses to alectinib and lorlatinib, relapsed with detection of on-target ALK kinase domain mutations (F1174V, I1171N) and MYC amplification on progression.
Conclusions
These cases expand the landscape of noncanonical ALK fusions in NSCLC which are responsive to approved ALK TKIs and offer insights into oncogenic and resistance mechanisms. Comprehensive molecular workup, including RNA-based NGS, is essential for detecting rare but actionable ALK rearrangements and optimizing therapeutic strategy. NGS of CSF was a valuable tool for the detection of clinically suspected leptomeningeal disease and disease monitoring.
Keywords: ALK fusion, anaplastic lymphoma kinase, NSCLC, novel fusion partners, next-generation sequencing
Highlights
-
•
Novel oncogenic ALK fusions (ALK::ZFPM2 and ALK::TRIM24) respond to ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs).
-
•
Complete molecular workup with RNA next-generation sequencing (NGS) is key to detect noncanonical ALK fusions.
-
•
On-target and bypass mutations may confer resistance in ALK fusion-positive NSCLC.
-
•
Cerebrospinal fluid NGS helped detect clinically suspected leptomeningeal disease.
Introduction
ALK fusions are actionable targets in many cancer types, particularly NSCLC, where it is detected in 3% to 4% of cases. Since the 2011 Food and Drug Administration approval of crizotinib as first-line therapy for ALK fusion-positive NSCLC, multiple next-generation ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) (such as alectinib and lorlatinib) have delivered substantial efficacy gains. In ALEX, alectinib extended median progression-free survival (PFS) from 10.9 months with crizotinib to 34.8 months, and median overall survival (OS) was not reached with alectinib versus 57.4 months with crizotinib at 5-year follow-up.1 In the 5-year follow-up of CROWN, which compared lorlatinib with crizotinib in a similar first-line population, median PFS remained not reached with lorlatinib versus 9.1 months with crizotinib, whereas OS data were still immature.2
The most common ALK fusion in NSCLC is EML4::ALK; however, many other 5′ fusion partners have been reported.3 The 5′ fusion partner may influence the intrinsic properties, oncogenic potential, and sensitivity of the fusion protein to ALK TKIs.4 Investigation of novel ALK fusion proteins and their associated clinical behavior and treatment response may thus help us better understand oncogenesis in ALK fusion-positive (ALK+) cancers and beyond, as many fusion partners are also observed in non-ALK fusion-driven cancers. We report the discovery of two novel ALK fusions ZFPM2::ALK and TRIM24::ALK, their clinical response to ALK TKIs, and potential modes of resistance.
Ethics Approval
The requirement for informed consent was waived by the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center Institutional Review Board (IRB No. 16‑1431) due to the retrospective nature of the study and use of de‑identified data.
Case 1: ZFPM2::ALK
A 69-year-old female never-smoker presented in 2019 with shortness of breath and chest pain (Fig. 1A). Cross-sectional imaging revealed a 4-cm left upper lobe mass, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion, and osseous metastases in the axial and appendicular skeletons (Fig. 1B). Endobronchial biopsy confirmed lung adenocarcinoma (TTF-1 positive, p40 negative) with ALK immunohistochemistry (IHC; clone D5F3) positivity (diffuse labeling in tumor cells); PD-L1 IHC (clone E1L3N) was negative. Based on the positive ALK IHC, alectinib (first-line standard of care at the time) was initiated within 2 weeks of tissue diagnosis at 600 mg twice daily. A partial response (per treating clinician) was achieved at 8 weeks, with a decrease in the left upper lobe mass from 4.1 cm × 2.6 cm to 2.8 cm × 1.5 cm and decreased mediastinal lymphadenopathy. DNA-based next-generation sequencing (NGS) via MSK-IMPACT performed on the initial biopsy sample revealed a ZFPM2::ALK fusion, BCL2L11 mutation, and MSI1 splicing variant. Archer-targeted RNA sequencing was performed but did not detect the ZFPM2::ALK fusion due to suboptimal sample quality.
Owing to diarrhea and fatigue at 2 months, alectinib was reduced to 450 mg twice daily. At 20 months on alectinib, the patient developed progression in fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid sternal metastases, which were palliatively irradiated. At 27 months on alectinib, the patient developed persistent headache, prompting brain imaging which was negative on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT); however, a lumbar puncture confirmed leptomeningeal disease (LMD). Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) was sent for NGS testing. The patient was transitioned to lorlatinib 100 mg daily with initial stable disease and mild improvement in headache and received 2 weeks of proton craniospinal irradiation (CSI) on a clinical trial. NGS performed on cell-free DNA from CSF before lorlatinib initiation revealed persistent ZFPM2::ALK fusion with a newly acquired CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion. Despite proton CSI and change in therapy, the patient developed clinical progression after 2 months on lorlatinib, with worsening neurologic symptoms, including increased hearing loss, mild intermittent confusion, gait instability, headache, and fecal incontinence. Repeat lumbar puncture revealed persistent LMD. She was transitioned to comfort care and died at 32 months from initial diagnosis.
Molecular Discussion
The novel ZFPM2::ALK fusion t(2;8)(p23.2;q23.1)(chr2:g.29447902::chr8:g.106384092) involves ZFPM2 exon 1 and the ALK kinase domain (exons 20–29) and was predicted to be in-frame and pathogenic on NGS based on the predicted structure (Fig. 1C). Positive ALK staining by IHC further supports its oncogenicity. Moreover, this fusion was an actionable target as demonstrated by the response to ALK TKI therapy.
ZFPM2 (Zinc Finger Protein, FOG family member 2) is a transcriptional cofactor involved in regulating gene expression during development and is expressed primarily in the ovary and endometrium and at low-to-moderate levels in other tissues, including the lung. ZFPM2 exon 1 (N-terminal partner) contains the 5′ untranslated region (UTR) which plays a crucial role in the regulation of gene expression by influencing mRNA stability and translation efficiency, most importantly is downstream of the ZFPM2 promoter. In contrast to EML4::ALK and NPM1::ALK, ZFPM2 exon 1 does not contain canonical dimerization domains.5,6 Further investigation would better characterize the mechanism of this pathogenic fusion.
On progression in the leptomeninges, CSF NGS did not reveal on-target ALK mutations, however, the presence of homozygous deletion of tumor suppressor and cell cycle regulator CDKN2A/B may have contributed to bypass resistance with loss of cell cycle control. Retrospective analysis of the CSF sample did not support homozygous deletion of the neighboring MTAP, and IHC did not support MTAP loss. Although concurrent ALK fusion and MTAP deletion have been reported, treatment-emergent MTAP deletion concurrent with CDKN2A/B deletion has only been reported in EGFR-mutated NSCLC in the setting of osimertinib resistance and should be assessed for at progression.7
Case 2: TRIM24::ALK
A 41-year-old male former smoker (2 pack-years, quit approximately 20 y prior) presented initially in 2017 with persistent cough and was found to have a large lung mass on CT scan. Staging imaging revealed metastases to mediastinal and abdominal lymph nodes, bone, and brain. Endobronchial biopsy identified adenocarcinoma with mucinous features, a cribriform and acinar pattern, and psammomatous calcification. ALK IHC (clone D5F3) was positive with weak diffuse staining, and fluorescence in situ hybridization performed at an outside facility was positive for ALK gene rearrangement. NGS was not initially performed.
The patient was started on alectinib 600 mg twice daily (Fig. 2A) with a partial response (per treating clinician) in all areas of disease including near resolution of a 0.6 cm brain lesion at 2.5 months (Fig. 2B). Oligoprogression in T4 and T5 vertebra was treated with stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT; at 17 and 21 mo, respectively), and the patient underwent T3 to T5 decompression for epidural disease and reirradiation (at 29 mo) for worsening epidural extension (epidural spinal cord compression, ESCC grade 1C) and SBRT to a left lower lobe lesion. Surgical biopsy confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma with mucinous features. At 32 months on alectinib, imaging revealed systemic progression of disease with a new FDG-avid left lower lobe subcentimeter lesion and thoracic adenopathy, recurrence in the spine, and increased brain metastases. The patient was transitioned to lorlatinib 100 mg daily with a partial response. After 12 months on lorlatinib (3.7 y from diagnosis), new and increased pulmonary metastases were noted; an endobronchial biopsy result revealed poorly differentiated non–small cell carcinoma, favoring adenocarcinoma.
DNA-based NGS via MSK-IMPACT revealed two ALK kinase domain alterations (F1174V on exon 22 and I1171N on exon 23), an ALK structural variant of undetermined significance (SVUS, c.3172+255:ALK_chr2:g.112450867inv), a TP53 DNA-binding domain mutation (H193R), and CDKN2Ap16 alteration (R80∗). Reflex RNA-anchored multiplex polymerase chain reaction detected an in-frame TRIM24::ALK fusion (Fig. 2C; exon 12 of TRIM24 and exon 20 of ALK). Carboplatin, pemetrexed, and bevacizumab were initiated with initial response after 5 weeks; however, disease progressed after 5 months. He was switched to docetaxel for 1 month before enrolling onto a trial of lorlatinib in combination with a SHP2 inhibitor (based on bypass blockade rationale). He came off study after 2 months due to progression and was started on gemcitabine and vinorelbine with rapid progression after 1 month.
At this time, plasma circulating tumor DNA detected the previously observed ALK SVUS, TP53 and CDKN2A alterations, and a new MYC amplification (fold change 2.3). The patient was transitioned to brigatinib (an alternate ALK TKI with reported sensitivity to the detected ALK kinase domain alterations) with a mixed response on initial imaging and a biopsy of a progressing liver lesion ruling out small cell transformation. NGS of the liver biopsy did not suggest small cell transformation and recapitulated prior NGS findings, including MYC amplification (fold change 4.8), as well as new LYN S104F, PIK3R2 X660_splice, RPS6KB2 I240V, and KDM6A intragenic duplication (c.226-17898_c.1082dup). The patient experienced rapid progression in the following months despite additional chemotherapy (vinblastine and mitomycin) and was hospitalized for rapid clinical deterioration (renal failure, large-volume pleural effusions, pain) at which point he was transitioned to comfort care. He died 4.8 years from initial diagnosis.
Molecular Discussion
Although NGS was not performed until progression after alectinib and lorlatinib, the detected TRIM24::ALK fusion was postulated to be the original oncogenic driver as evidenced by the response to ALK TKI therapy and detection of on-target resistance mutations (F1174V, I1171N). TRIM24 encodes a nuclear protein (transcription intermediary factor 1-alpha) that functions as transcriptional coactivator through interaction with numerous nuclear receptors. Although not previously reported in an ALK fusion, TRIM24 has been reported as an oncogenic fusion partner with NTRK2, NTRK3, RET, and MET.8, 9, 10 Each prior case similarly involved exon 12, which contains the 5′ coiled-coil dimerization and B-Box zinc finger domains of TRIM24, likely resulting in the constitutive activation of the paired kinase, similar to how the coiled-coil domain from EML4 facilitates constitutive ALK dimerization and activation.5
The two ALK kinase domain alterations observed have previously been reported. F1174V (on exon 22) confers resistance to ceritinib but is sensitive to alectinib, lorlatinib, and brigatinib; 1171N (on exon 23) confers resistance to alectinib but is sensitive to lorlatinib and brigatinib.11 It is unclear whether these two ALK kinase domain mutations synergize via compound in-cis resistance; however, the emergence of MYC amplification is a previously reported bypass resistance mechanism in ALK+ NSCLC and confers chemotherapy resistance.12,13 Multiple experimental therapies targeting MYC are currently in development.14
TRIM24 was poorly represented on the DNA NGS panel, so the ALK partner breakpoint initially mapped to an unknown locus of the intergenic region adjacent to ANAPC1 and was initially classified as a SVUS. Archer’s RNA-based NGS unambiguously resolved the fusion partner, overcoming the DNA assay’s limited breakpoint resolution and annotation. These findings underscore the necessity of RNA-based NGS for definitive identification and classification of rare gene fusions.
This patient’s clinical course illustrates how evolving, lesion-level resistance under second-generation ALK inhibition with alectinib can culminate in rapid clinical decline despite subsequent lorlatinib, consistent with polyclonal escape.
Although first-line administration of alectinib was consistent with contemporaneous standard of care in both above-mentioned cases, the evolution of disease in these two cases may have been altered with frontline administration of the now widely used lorlatinib. The CROWN study comparing first-line lorlatinib versus crizotinib supports the principle that earlier administration of a highly potent, CNS-penetrant, broad-coverage ALK inhibitor can reduce intracranial progression and potentially delay subclonal expansion, which is relevant to therapeutic sequencing in patients at high CNS risk.2
Conclusions
ZFPM2::ALK and TRIM24::ALK are two previously unreported oncogenic ALK fusions responsive to ALK TKI therapy. CSF NGS may be a useful tool to assess for bypass mechanisms in imaging-negative CNS progression. Reflex testing with RNA-based NGS is critical to complete molecular workup in cases with negative or indeterminate DNA NGS testing results.
